lessons.title: Offside: the blue line rule
lessons.objective: State what makes an entry offside.

payload.prompt: If both skates cross the blue line before the puck fully crosses, it is offside. True or false?

scene.alt: An attacker with both skates over the blue line as the puck remains in the neutral zone.

explanation.correct: Correct. That is the offside rule: both skates over the leading edge before the puck fully crosses.
explanation.incorrect: Offside is when both skates completely cross the blue line before the puck does. This is the definition.
explanation.sayThisLine: Both skates over the line before the puck, that's offside.

payload.prompt: One skate touching the blue line keeps you onside. True or false?

scene.alt: A skater with one blade on the blue line as the puck approaches.

explanation.correct: True. A skate on the line is onside. You must be completely over (both skates past the line) to be offside.
explanation.incorrect: If one skate touches the line, you are onside. Only both skates fully crossing the line makes you offside.
explanation.sayThisLine: Skate on the line is fine, both skates over is offside.

payload.prompt: Soccer also has offside. Is the hockey rule the same?

options.text: Yes, exactly the same rule
No. Hockey is about the blue line and skates; soccer is about the last defender and involvement.
Similar but slightly different

explanation.correct: Right. Hockey offside is mechanical (blue line + both skates). Soccer offside is about players and involvement. Do not mix them up.
explanation.incorrect: These are completely different rules. Hockey: blue line and skates. Soccer: last defender and active play. Know the difference.
explanation.sayThisLine: Hockey offside is the blue line, not like soccer at all.

payload.prompt: Match the concept to its role in offside.

pairs.definition: The boundary of the offensive zone; both skates crossing it before the puck means offside.
The edge of the blue line closer to the attacking zone where the offside judgment is made.
The offside rule requires both to cross completely for the violation to occur.

explanation.summary: Offside prevents pure cherry-picking near the goal; you must enter with or after the puck.
explanation.sayThisLine: Offside is about the blue line and when your skates cross it.

payload.prompt: Can a player be offside in the neutral zone?

options.text: Yes, if they are ahead of the puck
No, offside only applies at the blue line into the offensive zone
Only if they are past center ice

explanation.correct: Right. Offside is called when entering the offensive zone at the blue line. The neutral zone has no offside rule.
explanation.incorrect: Offside is a zone-entry rule. The neutral zone is free; you go offside when entering the offensive zone early.

lessons.title: Be the linesman: offside
lessons.objective: Call offside plays correctly at real speed.

payload.prompt: When does the linesman blow the whistle for offside?

options.text: After the offside player touches the puck
Immediately when the rule is violated (both skates over before puck)
Only if the offside player tries to score

explanation.correct: Right. The linesman calls it as soon as it happens, stopping play immediately.
explanation.incorrect: Offside is called the moment both skates cross before the puck, not after. The linesman stops it right away.
explanation.sayThisLine: Blow it when it happens, don't wait for the touch.

payload.prompt: Linesmen stand on the side of the ice to get the best angle on whether skates are over the line. True or false?

scene.alt: A linesman positioned on the side of the ice, looking perpendicular to the blue line.

explanation.correct: True. Position is everything in offside calls. The linesman moves to get the clearest sight line.
explanation.incorrect: Linesman positioning is critical. They move to the side to see if skates have crossed the line.

payload.prompt: Match the role to who does it.

pairs.definition: One of two officials stationed on the sides who watch for offside and icing.
When an attacker enters the offensive zone before the puck with both skates over the blue line.
Linesman raises the flag to indicate offside; the referee confirms and stops play.

explanation.summary: The linesman is the expert on offside because position is everything; they see it first.
explanation.sayThisLine: The linesman calls offside, not the ref.

payload.prompt: A common offside mistake: thinking that involvement in play matters. Does it?

options.text: Yes, if you don't touch it, you are not offside
No. Offside is about positioning when entering the zone, not involvement.
Only if the ref saw it

explanation.correct: Right. Offside is purely about skate position and the puck timing. It does not matter if you touch it.
explanation.incorrect: Offside is positional. You can be offside and not touch the puck. The rule is automatic based on positioning.

lessons.title: Delayed offside and tagging up
lessons.objective: Explain why play sometimes continues after an early entry.

payload.prompt: Order the delayed offside events correctly.

items.text: Attacker enters zone early (both skates over)
Defense gains control of the puck
Linesman does not blow whistle immediately
Attacker tags up and can re-enter

explanation.correct: Perfect. That is delayed offside: let play go while defense has the puck.
explanation.incorrect: Delayed offside happens when defense controls after early entry. Linesman waits to see if attacking team gets it.
explanation.sayThisLine: Defense has it, so delayed offside, no whistle yet.

payload.prompt: If an offside attacker waits while the defense has the puck, the linesman blows the whistle immediately. True or false?

scene.alt: An attacker waits in the zone while a defender has possession.

explanation.correct: False. If the defense has control, the linesman does not blow it. Play continues (delayed offside).
explanation.incorrect: Delayed offside means the linesman delays the whistle while the defense has the puck. Play goes on.

payload.prompt: Match the term to what it means in delayed offside.

pairs.definition: An offside attacker touches the blue line to become onside again.
The defense shoots the puck out of the zone, ending the delayed offside situation.
After tagging up, the attacker can participate in play again.

explanation.summary: Tag-up is the mechanism that brings an offside player back into the game.
explanation.sayThisLine: She tagged up at the line, so now she can play again.

payload.prompt: If the attacking team touches the puck while someone is still offside, what happens?

options.text: Delayed offside ends and play continues normally
The linesman immediately calls offside
Only if the offside player touched it

explanation.correct: Right. When the attacking team gets the puck, if someone is still offside, the linesman calls it right then.
explanation.incorrect: Delayed offside ends when the attacking team touches the puck. If someone is offside at that moment, the call is made.

lessons.title: Icing, and why teams hate it
lessons.objective: Describe what icing is and its penalty.

payload.prompt: What is icing?

options.text: A penalty for hitting someone
Shooting from behind center ice to the goal line untouched
Deliberately shooting over the glass

explanation.correct: Right. Icing is a desperation clear from your own side of center to the goal line.
explanation.incorrect: Icing: shoot from your side of center to the opponent's goal line without anyone touching it.

payload.prompt: Icing gives the other team a power play. True or false?

scene.alt: A puck sliding down the ice and being called icing.

explanation.correct: False. Icing is not a penalty. No power play. The cost is: faceoff in your zone and you cannot change players.
explanation.incorrect: Icing is a stoppage, not a penalty. No power play, just a bad restart position.

payload.prompt: Match what happens after icing is called.

pairs.definition: The faceoff happens in the zone of the team that iced it.
The team that iced cannot swap players; they must defend with the same line.
The same players stay on the ice, creating fatigue and pressure in your own end.

explanation.summary: Icing is self-inflicted pain: bad restart plus no fresh legs.
explanation.sayThisLine: They iced it and now they can't change, so they are stuck.

payload.prompt: When is icing most dangerous for your team?

options.text: Any time, icing is always bad
When you're losing late in the game and need to score
During a power play when you are already down a player

explanation.correct: Right. Late in a losing game, icing wastes time and forces a defensive restart.
explanation.incorrect: Icing hurts most when you are losing and need offensive time. It stops your momentum.

payload.prompt: Shooting the puck off the glass behind the goal line counts as icing if it goes untouched. True or false?

scene.alt: A puck bounces off the glass behind the goal line.

explanation.correct: True. Where it comes off (glass or ice) doesn't matter. Untouched past the goal line is icing.
explanation.incorrect: Icing is icing whether the puck bounces or slides. The key is: untouched to the goal line.

lessons.title: Be the linesman: hybrid icing
lessons.objective: Decide when hybrid icing is called.

payload.prompt: How does the linesman call hybrid icing?

options.text: When a player first touches the puck
When the linesman judges a defender will reach the faceoff dots first
When the puck reaches the goal line

explanation.correct: Right. The linesman blows it based on positioning before anyone touches it.
explanation.incorrect: Hybrid icing is judgment-based. The linesman calls it when it is clear the defender will win the race.

payload.prompt: Hybrid icing was introduced to prevent high-speed collisions at the boards. True or false?

scene.alt: Two players racing toward the boards at high speed.

explanation.correct: True. The old race-to-the-puck rule caused injuries. Hybrid icing is safer.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, hybrid icing was a safety improvement. No high-speed races needed.

payload.prompt: Match the icing style to how it worked.

pairs.definition: Old rule: any attacker touch canceled icing; led to high-speed races.
Current rule: linesman judges positioning before anyone touches; no race needed.
Both rules aim to stop icing clears, but hybrid does it safely.

explanation.summary: Hybrid icing is modern and safer than the old touch-up rule.
explanation.sayThisLine: Hybrid icing means no one races anymore.

payload.prompt: In hybrid icing, if the attacker is clearly going to reach the puck first, what happens?

options.text: Icing is called anyway
Icing is not called; it is a good clear
The ref asks the linesman

explanation.correct: Right. If the attacker gets there first, no icing. Play continues.
explanation.incorrect: Hybrid icing is called only if the defender would reach the dots first. Otherwise play continues.

lessons.title: When icing does not apply
lessons.objective: Know why a shorthanded team can freely ice.

payload.prompt: A team on the penalty kill (down a player) can ice the puck without a stoppage. True or false?

scene.alt: A shorthanded team clears the puck from their defensive zone with 4 skaters on ice.

explanation.correct: True. The shorthanded team has an icing exemption. It is relief built into the rules.
explanation.incorrect: Penalty-kill teams do not get called for icing. They need relief because they are already down a player.

payload.prompt: Can a team on the power play (the attacking team) ice without it being called?

options.text: Yes, same as the penalty-kill team
No, icing is called against them like any other team
Only if their power play is failing

explanation.correct: Right. The power-play team does not get an icing exemption. Only the shorthanded team does.
explanation.incorrect: Only penalty-kill teams can ice freely. The power-play team is held to the normal icing rule.

payload.prompt: Match the concept to why icing exemption exists.

pairs.definition: Down a player because a teammate is in the penalty box.
Built-in fairness: ability to clear the puck freely to survive the power play.
The penalty-kill goal: run out the clock and get the power play over.

explanation.summary: Icing exemption is fairness: you are already at a disadvantage, so you get one break.
explanation.sayThisLine: On the penalty kill, icing is allowed, that is the rule.

payload.prompt: If the puck is deflected before reaching the goal line, it is not icing. True or false?

scene.alt: A puck is touched (deflected) by a player's stick before crossing the goal line.

explanation.correct: True. Any touch cancels icing. Untouched is the requirement.
explanation.incorrect: Icing requires the puck to go untouched. A deflection negates it.

payload.prompt: Besides the penalty-kill exemption, when else is an icing clear ignored?

options.text: In overtime any time
If the puck is touched by any player before the goal line
When the goalie shoots it

explanation.correct: Right. Any touch of the puck cancels icing. If someone on either team touches it, icing is not called.
explanation.incorrect: Icing is only called when the puck is completely untouched from behind center to the goal line.

lessons.title: Goal, no goal: review and challenges
lessons.objective: Explain what coaches can challenge and what it costs.

payload.prompt: What can a coach challenge?

options.text: Any goal they think is wrong
Offside on entry, goalie interference, or a goal that should have counted
Only goalie interference

explanation.correct: Right. Three main things: offside entry, goalie interference, and goals waved off incorrectly.
explanation.incorrect: Coaches can challenge these specific situations: offside, goalie interference, and overturned goals.

payload.prompt: A failed challenge costs the team its timeout. True or false?

scene.alt: A coach throws the red flag and the video review upholds the call.

explanation.correct: True. Lose the challenge, lose the timeout. It is a real cost.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, a failed challenge is expensive. You lose your timeout for the rest of the game.

payload.prompt: If a challenge is successful (video overturns the call), what is the cost?

options.text: You lose your timeout anyway
You keep your timeout and can challenge again if allowed
The other team gets a power play

explanation.correct: Right. Winning a challenge has no cost. You keep your timeout.
explanation.incorrect: A successful challenge is rewarded: you keep the timeout and often can challenge again.

payload.prompt: Match the review term to what it means.

pairs.definition: The coach throws the red flag to request video review of a specific play.
Video overturns the on-ice call; coach keeps timeout and the goal stands or is reversed.
Video upholds the call; coach loses timeout and the goal stands as called.

explanation.summary: Challenging is risky: win and you keep the timeout, lose and it costs you.
explanation.sayThisLine: The challenge worked, the goal was offside.

payload.prompt: A coach thinks a goal is offside in the third period of a close game. Should they challenge?

options.text: Yes, always challenge if you think you're right
Think twice; you may need your timeout later
No, challenges are rarely successful

explanation.correct: Right. Strategy matters. Challenges are powerful but expensive if wrong.
explanation.incorrect: Challenging late in a close game is risky. You need to know if you're confident or you might lose that timeout.

lessons.title: The crease and goalie contact
lessons.objective: Explain why some goals get waved off.

payload.prompt: Light incidental contact between an attacker and the goalie always cancels the goal. True or false?

scene.alt: Slight contact between an attacker and a goalie in the crease.

explanation.correct: False. Light contact is okay. Only contact that impairs the save is interference.
explanation.incorrect: Goalie interference requires the contact to actually prevent the save. Light touch alone is not enough.

payload.prompt: What makes contact interference (and cancels the goal)?

options.text: Any attacker in the crease
Contact that prevents the goalie from making a save
An attacker standing still in front of the net

explanation.correct: Right. It is about whether the contact prevented the save.
explanation.incorrect: Goalie interference is about the contact's effect. Does it prevent the goalie from stopping the puck? If yes, no goal.

payload.prompt: Match the concept to its role in crease contact.

pairs.definition: The blue painted area in front of the goal; attackers can enter but cannot impair the goalie.
Touching the goalie is okay if it does not affect their ability to move or save.
Prevent the goalie from being in position or from moving to make a save.

explanation.summary: The crease is shared space; interference is about the impact of contact.
explanation.sayThisLine: In the crease but not impaired the save, it is a goal.

payload.prompt: Attacker pushes goalie away and puck goes in. It is a goal. True or false?

scene.alt: An attacker pushing a goalie away from the post as the puck slides in.

explanation.correct: False. The goal is waved off for interference. The attacker moved the goalie.
explanation.incorrect: If an attacker's action prevents the save (pushing the goalie), the goal does not count no matter where the puck goes.

payload.prompt: Is it legal to stand in the crease and screen the goalie?

options.text: No, any attacker in the crease blocks the goal
Yes, if you do not push or move the goalie
Only if the puck is in the air

explanation.correct: Right. Screening (standing in front) is legal. Interference is about contact that prevents the save.
explanation.incorrect: Attackers can legally stand in the crease and screen. It is only interference if they impair the goalie's movement.
